whyChoose.title: Why Act Sooner Rather Than Later

items.title: California's Filing Deadline
items.desc: California law generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury claim. That window can shrink to as little as six months if a government entity, like a public road authority, is involved.

items.title: Fault Doesn't Have to Be All-or-Nothing
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning you can still recover damages even if you were partly responsible for the accident. Your compensation is simply reduced by your share of fault, not eliminated.

items.title: No Cap on Pain and Suffering
items.desc: In ordinary injury cases, California places no limit on non-economic damages like pain, suffering, and emotional distress. That means your compensation isn't artificially capped by a statutory ceiling.

items.title: No Upfront Cost to You
items.desc: Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so there's no fee unless they recover money on your behalf. That structure lets you pursue a claim without paying out of pocket first.

items.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Rolling Hills?
items.answer: Under California law, you generally have two years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit. If your claim involves a government entity or public road, that deadline can be as short as six months, so it's wise to act early.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.answer: California uses a pure comparative fault system, so being partially at fault doesn't bar you from recovering compensation. Your total award is simply reduced by your percentage of fault.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to cluster in Rolling Hills?
items.answer: Public collision records show that Crenshaw Boulevard, Crest Road West, Pathfinder Road, and the 900 block of Silver Spur Road have the higher recorded collision counts in town. These are neutral public-record figures, not a judgment about any particular road.

items.question: Is there a cap on how much I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: No. In standard personal injury cases, California does not cap non-economic damages such as pain and suffering. Your recovery depends on the specifics of your case, not a statutory limit.

items.question: Will I have to pay anything upfront to get help?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service, and attorneys in our network work on a contingency basis. That means there's no fee unless they recover compensation for you.
